<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-signposted cases and followed format cleanly (correct Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 usage). CON's strongest line — that a social graph is third-party data, not user property, and that any transfer mechanism therefore requires nonconsensual disclosure — was a genuinely sharp category objection that PRO had to answer. PRO did answer it: it engineered a concrete mechanism (hashed-pointer matching, opt-in reconnection prompts, exclusion filters for blocked/minor accounts) analogized to real phone-number porting and to how GDPR-style portability regimes already operate, directly neutralizing the "map leaves without consent" charge rather than just asserting it away. CON's rejoinder — that any safeguard "rewrites the motion" — is a clever but ultimately thin textualist move; a reasonable reading of "legally required interoperable...transfer" easily accommodates privacy-preserving implementation, and CON never explained why safeguards are illegitimate rather than sensible regulatory design. Meanwhile PRO's pressure question ("what remedy do you offer for lock-in?") exposed a real gap: CON's answers (antitrust, competing on safety) don't restore the specific asset — existing connections — that portability targets, and PRO's closing crystallized that gap cleanly. CON never squarely rebutted the "exit-threat disciplines incumbents even without switching" mechanism, leaving PRO's structural case for a legal mandate more intact at the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's hashed-pointer/reconnection design (B4.1–B4.3) directly answering CON's consent-collapse objection, paired with PRO's closing turn on "antitrust doesn't return your ten years of connections" against CON's non-mechanism remedies, was the decisive exchange.</best_rebuttal>
